title: Universal Grammar & Acquisition Debates

pts: Chomsky's Universal Grammar theory argues humans possess an innate, biologically endowed set of grammatical principles underlying all languages.
This explains the rapid, robust way children acquire their first language despite limited and imperfect input — the 'poverty of the stimulus' argument.
This remains one of the most influential, and most contested, theories in the history of linguistics.

blocks.x: What do you know that nobody taught you?

items: Give pairs six sentence cards, some possible and some impossible in English (see model language).
Pairs sort them into ‘possible’ and ‘impossible’ in two minutes, without discussing rules.
Ask: who taught you that the impossible ones are impossible?
Repeat with parallel sentences in a shared language such as Kannada, Hindi or Telugu.
Introduce Chomsky’s claim and ask trainees to paraphrase it for a parent.
In a DIET in-service session, invite faculty from other language departments to supply examples.
For B2–C1 learners of English, use the sort as a language-awareness warmer.
Support: give the possible version of each pair first, so trainees compare rather than judge in isolation.
Challenge: trainees write two further pairs that show the same hidden knowledge.

lines: Who did Meena say that Arjun met? (possible)
Who did Meena meet Arjun and? (impossible)
Children seem ready to find certain kinds of pattern in language, so they know more than anyone has directly taught them.
T: Did anyone ever tell you not to say ‘Who did Meena meet Arjun and?’
S1: Never. It just sounds broken.
T: That is Chomsky’s puzzle. The debate is about where that knowledge comes from.

body: Purpose: to show the core UG claim as a gap. Content: a child receiving a narrow stream of speech bubbles on the left and producing a much wider fan of sentences on the right; a small box labelled ‘endowment?’ sits in the child’s head. Style: clean diagram; the question mark signals a claim, not a fact. Board version: a narrow arrow in, a wide arrow out, and a box with a question mark.

points.h: The Poverty of the Stimulus Argument
pts: Children acquire complex grammatical knowledge they seemingly couldn't have learned solely from the limited, often flawed input they receive.
This gap between input and output is argued to require some innate grammatical scaffolding to explain.
Critics argue this gap has been overstated, or can be explained by sufficiently powerful general learning mechanisms instead.

v: Teacher education; trainee teachers or DIET faculty
Children’s storybooks or a small corpus

items: Present the classic example: children form Is the boy who is singing happy? and not Is the boy who singing is happy?, although a simple ‘move the first is’ rule predicts the error (Crain and Nakayama 1987).
Explain the argument: children rarely hear the evidence needed to rule out the simpler, wrong rule.
Half the group argues that such evidence is too rare; half searches twenty pages of storybooks or a corpus for it.
Groups report. Introduce the critique that such evidence may be less rare than assumed (Pullum and Scholz 2002), and the reply that rarity is only part of the argument.
Each trainee writes one balanced summary sentence.
Search a Kannada or Hindi children’s book and discuss whether the question even arises in a verb-final language.
Support: provide a short text with two target sentences hidden in it.
Challenge: trainees summarize the method of Pullum and Scholz (2002).

blocks.x: A balanced summary (written for this book):

lines: Children’s questions show that they follow structure, not word order; how much of that knowledge must be innate is still debated.
A: We found none in twenty pages.
B: Twenty pages is not what a child hears in four years.
A: So absence in our sample does not prove absence in the input.

blocks.x: This is the reasoning about sampling that Unit 81 applied to classroom research.

pts: The Principles and Parameters framework proposed UG consists of universal principles plus language-specific parameters that get 'set' by exposure.
This offered a formal mechanism for explaining both cross-linguistic universals and specific-language variation.
This framework has itself evolved substantially since its original formulation, within ongoing generative linguistics.

v: Parallel sentences in English and one Indian language

items: Write three English sentences: a verb with an object, a phrase with a preposition, and a sentence with a pronoun subject.
Learners translate them into their home language in language groups.
Groups compare: where does the verb come? Where does the word for ‘from’ come? Can the subject be left out?
Introduce parameters: one setting for head direction, one for null subjects.
Learners predict one error an Indian learner of English might make because of these settings.
With trainee teachers, add Urdu or Konkani and build a table of settings.
Support: provide the translations and ask only for the comparison.
Challenge: learners find a case where the home language does not follow its main setting.

lines: Is coming tomorrow. (a dropped subject carried into English)

blocks.x: English is head-initial and requires a subject; Hindi, Kannada and Tamil are largely head-final and allow the subject to be dropped. Parameters explain why languages differ systematically, not just word by word (Chomsky 1981).

Style: clean infographic, labels as well as colours. Board version: a two-column table with ticks.

points.sub: Does it still apply to adults?
pts: Whether Universal Grammar remains fully, partially, or not at all accessible to adult second-language learners is the field's central UG-related debate.
This directly shapes how much explicit instruction can realistically achieve versus how much must be left to implicit, UG-guided processes.
The following card surveys the three main positions in this specific debate.

v: Teacher education; trainee or in-service teachers

items: Mark a line across the room from ‘Strongly agree’ to ‘Strongly disagree’.
Read a statement about adult learning; participants stand where their belief lies.
Invite one person from each end and one from the middle to explain.
After three statements, reveal that each matches a position in the UG access debate.
Participants note which position their classroom practice actually assumes.
In a fixed-bench hall, participants hold up cards numbered 1–5 instead of moving.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Adults can learn a language the way children do, given enough input.
After childhood, grammar can only be learned consciously, through rules.
Some parts of grammar come naturally to adults and some never do.
T: Where would you have stood ten years ago?
S1: Nearer ‘rules only’. My own training was all rules.
T: Unit 79 showed how our beliefs often come from how we were taught.

body: Purpose: to show a spread of beliefs as data. Content: a horizontal line with small figures clustered unevenly along it and three statements above. Style: friendly, non-judgemental. Board version: a line with initials along it.

items: Mentimeter (free plan) scale question for large or online groups.

blocks.x: Numbered cards held up at each statement.

points.h: Access Debates in Adult L2 Acquisition
pts: 'Full access' positions argue UG remains fully available to adult L2 learners, just as in L1 acquisition.
'No access' positions argue UG is only available during a critical developmental period, unavailable to adult learners.
'Partial access' positions occupy a middle ground, with ongoing debate about exactly which UG principles remain accessible.

v: Teacher education; trainee teachers or DIET faculty

items: In groups of three, each member receives one card: full access (Schwartz and Sprouse 1996), no access (Bley-Vroman 1989) or partial access.
Each member explains their position in two minutes.
Give each group a set of learner sentences.
For each sentence, each member explains how their position accounts for it.
Plenary: agree that each position fits some data better than others.
Use anonymized sentences from your own learners’ writing (Unit 49).
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

pts: Usage-based and cognitive-linguistic accounts (Unit 82) explain acquisition through general learning mechanisms, without positing an innate grammar module.
Connectionist and emergentist models offer yet another alternative, emphasising statistical pattern-learning from input.
This genuine multiplicity of competing explanations reflects the field's ongoing, unresolved theoretical complexity.

v: A developmental pattern; a short reading on usage-based learning

items: Present a common pattern: learners say I don’t know correctly long before they produce other negatives correctly (He not come).
Trainees explain it first with a UG account, then with a usage-based account (Unit 82).
Point out that frequent chunks are often learned whole and analysed later (Tomasello 2003).
Trainees list the teaching implication of each explanation and mark where they overlap.
Trainees collect examples of early chunks from younger siblings’ Kannada, Hindi or Tamil.
Support: provide both explanations and ask trainees to match them to sources.
Challenge: trainees design an observation that might tell the accounts apart.

lines: UG: the grammar develops according to principles; the chunk is stored separately until the system catches up.
Usage-based: I don’t know is heard thousands of times, so it is learned as a unit, and the pattern is extracted gradually.
Learners need plentiful meaningful input and practice with frequent patterns.

body: Purpose: to show one phenomenon through two theories. Content: one learner utterance under two magnifying lenses, ‘innate principles’ and ‘usage and chunks’, each with a caption. Style: even-handed. Board version: two circles over one sentence.

items: Miro (free plan, limited editable boards) for a two-column comparison.

points.h: Why This Debate Matters for Teaching
pts: Whether UG remains accessible to adult learners has real implications for how much explicit grammar instruction can realistically achieve.
This connects directly to Unit 6's deductive-versus-inductive grammar teaching debate, which partly reflects this deeper theoretical disagreement.
Teachers needn't resolve this debate to teach well, but awareness of it contextualises why grammar pedagogy itself remains contested.

v: One grammar point; two lesson plans

items: Choose one grammar point, for example the present perfect for experience.
Plan a deductive and an inductive lesson (Unit 6) and write the assumption behind each.
Teach one plan to one section and the other to a parallel section.
A week later, collect a short speaking or writing sample from both.
Discuss the results cautiously: two classes inform your decisions but cannot settle a theory.
In a DIET practicum, trainee pairs teach the two versions and observe each other (Unit 68).
Support: provide ready-made plans.
Challenge: trainees design a fairer comparison, controlling for time and teacher (Unit 81).

lines: Deductive: Explicit rules may compensate for reduced implicit learning in adolescents and adults.
Inductive: Learners who discover a pattern from examples notice it more deeply.
9A used the form more accurately a week later. But 9A also had the lesson in the morning. I cannot say the method caused the difference.

body: When trainees ask ‘Which theory is right?’, turn the question round: ‘What would you do differently if it were true?’ Many theoretical disagreements lead to similar classroom choices, and the differences that remain are the ones worth discussing.

pts: No consensus position has emerged, and the debate remains genuinely active within contemporary SLA and linguistics research.
This series has drawn on UG as one useful reference point (Unit 6) without treating it as the field's single settled truth.
This reflects the appropriate epistemic humility this entire tier has modelled throughout its theoretical content.

dek: Unit 86 of 100: returning to Chomsky's foundational theory in full depth — what Universal Grammar claims, what evidence supports it, and where genuine scholarly disagreement remains.

aims.x: This unit gives Universal Grammar the full treatment it has waited for since Unit 1 first mentioned Chomsky. It sets out what the theory claims, the evidence offered for it, how it was formalized, and the unresolved debate about whether adult learners still have access to it. It then asks the question that matters to teachers and teacher educators: what, if anything, should this debate change in a grammar lesson?
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: state the core claim of Universal Grammar (UG) accurately, without caricature;
explain the poverty of the stimulus argument and the main objections to it;
illustrate a parameter by comparing English with an Indian language;
summarize the full-access, no-access and partial-access positions on adult L2 acquisition;
compare UG with usage-based accounts of the same data;
relate the debate to the choice between explicit and implicit grammar teaching (Unit 6);
present a contested theory honestly in a teacher-education session.

why: Why this matters. This series has referenced Chomsky since its opening framing. This poster finally gives Universal Grammar the direct, thorough treatment it deserves.

background.x: In Aspects of the Theory of Syntax, Noam Chomsky (1965) distinguished a speaker’s underlying knowledge of language (competence) from its use in real situations (performance), and argued that linguistics should explain how every child comes to possess that knowledge. His answer was that children bring a rich, species-specific endowment to the task. The theory of that endowment is Universal Grammar: not the grammar of any one language, but the properties that constrain what a possible human grammar can be.

The theory has not stood still. The Principles and Parameters framework (Chomsky 1981) proposed fixed principles plus a small number of parameters set by experience, and later generative work has tried to reduce the innate component to very few operations. Teachers who learned ‘UG’ as a single fixed doctrine may be surprised by how much the generative tradition itself has revised.

For language teaching, the most consequential question is whether UG remains available after childhood. Lydia White (2003) reviews research suggesting that adult L2 grammars are constrained in ways input alone does not explain; Robert Bley-Vroman (1989) argued that adult learning is fundamentally different from child acquisition. Usage-based researchers such as Michael Tomasello (2003) explain acquisition through general learning mechanisms sensitive to frequency and pattern, with no dedicated grammar module. Unit 77 surveyed these competing models; this unit looks closely at one of them.

India offers a rich vantage point. Many Indian children acquire two or three languages before school, often including languages as different as Kannada or Tamil (verb-final, with postpositions) and English (verb-medial, with prepositions). NEP 2020 recommends the home language as the medium of instruction wherever possible, at least until Grade 5 (Ministry of Human Resource Development 2020), and NCF 2023 treats children’s languages as resources (NCERT 2023). Whatever one’s view of UG, this everyday multilingual competence is exactly what any acquisition theory must explain.

items: Accurate summary. A 150-word explanation of UG and the poverty of the stimulus argument for a new teacher, without overclaiming.
Parameter comparison. A table comparing English with one Indian language on two parameters, with one predicted learner error.
Position analysis. One learner error analysed from full-, partial- and no-access perspectives.
Hedged rewrite. Three overstated claims from real materials, rewritten with sources traced.
Before this unit, what did you believe UG claimed? Where did that belief come from?
Which position in the access debate does your grammar teaching actually assume?
How does knowing two or three Indian languages shape your view of what is ‘universal’?
When did you last present a theory to trainees as settled when it was not?
If the usage-based view were fully correct, what would you change in your teaching?
How can you model uncertainty for trainees without leaving them confused?

terms.def: In Chomsky’s (1965) theory, a speaker’s underlying knowledge of language, as distinct from performance, the actual use of language in real situations.

The view that adult second language learners still have access to Universal Grammar, so that their grammars are constrained by it even when first-language features transfer at the start (Schwartz and Sprouse 1996).
In Universal Grammar, the setting that decides whether heads such as verbs come before or after their complements. English is head-initial (read books); Kannada and Hindi are head-final.

In Universal Grammar, the parameter that determines whether a language allows subject pronouns to be omitted; Kannada and Hindi allow this, so learners may produce English sentences like ‘Is raining’.
The position that adult second-language learners have access to some but not all of Universal Grammar, for example to principles but not to parameter values that differ from the first language.
Chomsky’s argument that the language children hear is insufficient to explain the complex grammar they acquire, which suggests some innate knowledge of language.
Chomsky’s (1981) model of Universal Grammar, in which universal principles are shared by all languages and parameters are set differently in each language.

The principle that grammatical rules operate on hierarchical structures, not on the linear order of words. Children forming questions such as ‘Is the boy who is singing happy?’ appear to respect it without instruction (Crain and Nakayama 1987).
Chomsky’s proposal that humans have innate principles common to all languages, which constrain and guide language acquisition (Chomsky 1965). Its role in second language learning remains debated.

The view that language knowledge is built from the expressions people actually meet and use, through general cognitive abilities such as pattern-finding (Tomasello 2003). It emphasizes frequency, exposure and meaningful use.
